expected_evidence: Geological: anomalous spikes in cosmogenic nuclide production (10Be, 36Cl, 14C) in Greenland ice cores (GISP2/GRIP/NEEM) precisely at the Younger Dryas onset horizon (~12,900 cal BP), consistent with a burst of ionizing radiation rather than solar modulation alone.
Geological/geochemical: nitrate, ammonium, or other atmospheric-ionization chemical markers in the same ice layers, distinguishable from volcanic or solar-proton-event signatures.

Astronomical: identification of a supernova remnant with an age (~11,000-13,000 yr) and heliocentric distance close enough (roughly <1000 pc) to plausibly deliver a gamma-ray dose sufficient to affect Earth's atmosphere (e.g., candidate objects like the Vela SNR have been floated in speculative literature).
Astronomical/isotopic: a 60Fe or other supernova-nucleosynthesis-tracer anomaly in ice or deep-sea sediment layers dating to the same interval, as used for confirmed nearby-supernova epochs.
Material/paleoclimate: correlation of the isotopic/chemical anomaly with the independently dated onset of Younger Dryas cooling in the same or correlated ice-core/sediment records.
Genetic: population bottleneck signatures in contemporaneous fauna/flora consistent with a sudden radiation or climate shock (weak, low-resolution proxy).
Absence-of-evidence check: lack of confounding impact-related markers (platinum, iridium, spherules) that would instead favor a competing (bolide impact) hypothesis for the same cooling event.
response.rationale: The hypothesis is keyed to the Younger Dryas onset, so the younger-dryas row is the closest match to the unspecified period (the interval -12000 to -11001 covers the accepted YD onset ~12,900 cal BP). Its two most load-bearing evidence kinds, geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7), are both highly detectable: Greenland ice sheets (GISP2, GRIP, NEEM, NGRIP) preserve continuous, well-dated stratigraphy through and well before this interval, so any real cosmogenic-isotope or chemical-ionization spike at the YD boundary would very plausibly have survived and already been sampled by existing ice-core programs. Likewise, supernova remnants with ages of ~11,000-13,000 years remain observable today via X-ray/radio astronomy and isotopic (60Fe) tracers, so a genuine nearby event of this age is not the kind of evidence that would simply vanish — its absence in the literature is informative, not just a detectability artifact. Textual (0.0), linguistic (0.05), oral_tradition (0.1), and iconographic (0.1) evidence are essentially unobtainable because this predates writing and any traceable oral/iconographic tradition by millennia, so their absence should not be read as evidence against the hypothesis at all — it's a structural detectability floor, not falsification. Genetic evidence (0.3) is weak/coarse for this resolution and time depth. Given that the two channels most diagnostic for this specific mechanism (geological ice-core chemistry, astronomical remnant/isotope surveys) are both moderately-to-highly detectable and have in fact been searched by real paleoclimate and astrophysics research (model-prior, unverified in detail: mainstream studies have not found an unambiguous gamma-ray/supernova signature at the YD boundary, and the leading isotopic anomalies are usually attributed to solar activity or an unresolved cause), the 'inconclusive' status of this hypothesis is plausible on its own evidentiary merits rather than being an artifact of poor preservation. I set the aggregate detectability adjustment at 0.6, slightly below the average of the geological/astronomical rows, to reflect that while the physical archives survive, cleanly attributing an isotopic excursion specifically to a supernova gamma-ray flux (versus other radiation sources) is scientifically difficult even with surviving material.
